summary: Ubay bin Ka'b narrates that the Prophet taught him the virtue of Surah Faatiha as the seven often-repeated verses.
Anas relates that Abu Talha found the Prophet teaching the men of Suffa with a stone tied to his belly because of hunger.
Anas relates that Abu Moosa recited the Qur'aan at home, and that the Prophet, having heard him unseen, praised his recitation as one of the tunes of the family of Dawood.
notes: Opening sentence is OCR-garbled ('something remarkable of Abu He was sitting'); the meaning is clear.

summary: Anas relates how Umar questioned him about Abu Moosa and the people of Basrah, and Abu Rajaa Utaaridi describes Abu Moosa teaching the Qur'aan in the Basrah masjid.
notes: Two reports: Anas's account of Umar's questions, then Abu Rajaa Utaaridi's report of Abu Moosa teaching. The quote ends unclosed. 'Urnar' is OCR for Umar.

summary: Ali says that after the Prophet passed away he vowed not to take off his shawl until he had memorised the whole Qur'aan.
Maymoon reports that Abdullaah bin Umar took four years to learn Surah Baqara.
notes: The text gives only 'Maymoon', so the approved 'maymoon' is used and is unsure; Maymoon bin Mahraan (maymoon-bin-mahraan) may be the intended narrator. Trailing OCR debris ignored.

summary: Salmaan recites Surah Yusuf to a crowd in the Madaa'in masjid, and when most of them leave he rebukes those who prefer a lecture to the Book of Allaah.
notes: The reporter is an unnamed man of the Ashja tribe and the crowd is unnamed, so neither is listed.

summary: Abdullaah bin Mas'ood teaches each verse of the Qur'aan to the people who come to his house each morning and tells them it is better than everything the sun rises upon.
notes: Two reports: the habit of teaching each verse, then 'Another narration states' a longer version of the morning teaching.

summary: Abdullaah bin Mas'ood tells the people to hold fast to the Qur'aan as Allaah's laden tablecloth, since knowledge is acquired only through study.
notes: 'Abduilaah' is OCR for Abdullaah.

summary: Another narration has Abdullaah bin Mas'ood say that a house without the Book of Allaah is like a deserted house and that Shaytaan leaves a house where Surah Baqarah is recited.
Umar tells a man who often came to his door to go and study the Book of Allaah, and the man later says the Book has made him independent of Umar's door.
notes: The narrator is given only as 'Hadhrat Hasan'; the approved 'hasan-bin-abil-hasan' (Hasan al-Basri) is assumed and is unsure. The man is unnamed.

summary: Umar says every Muslim man should learn six Surahs, two each for the Fajr, Maghrib and Isha salaah.
Umar names the Surahs that should be learnt, citing Miswar bin Makhrama, a letter to governors reported by Haaritha bin Mudarrib, and a further narration on teaching Surah Noor to women.
notes: Three narrations: Miswar's (Baqarah, Nisaa, Maa'idah, Hajj, Noor), Haaritha's (Nisaa, Ahzaab, Noor), and an unattributed 'another narration' (Baraa'ah, Noor for women). 'Sgi' after Miswar's name is OCR debris.

summary: Abu Rayhaana complains that he finds the Qur'aan hard to learn, and the Prophet advises him not to take on more than he can manage and to pray much nafl salaah; Umayrah reports that he used to make much sajdah at Asqalaan.
notes: Two reports: the Prophet's advice to Abu Rayhaana, then Umayrah's report about Asqalaan. 'ticS-f' after the Prophet's name is OCR debris.

summary: Qaradha bin Ka'b reports that Umar, on the journey to Iraq, asked the Sahabah to keep the people occupied with the Qur'aan and narrate few Ahadeeth, and Qaradha repeated that prohibition when asked to narrate in Iraq.
notes: The Sahabah who travelled with Umar are unnamed.

summary: Another narration has Umar tell the Sahabah not to preoccupy the people with Ahadeeth, since that will stop them mastering the Qur'aan, and gives the same reason for the journey as before.
notes: The text ends 'The rest of the narration is like the one above', so it depends on n02815 for the rest of the account.

summary: A freed slave of Abdullaah bin Umar relates how Umar had Sabeegh, who questioned the mutashaabih verses, beaten with date-palm branches and ordered the people to shun him until Abu Moosa reported he had reformed; a second narration, from Sulaymaan bin Yasaar, gives an account of Sabeegh being beaten by Umar in Madinah until he said his doubts had gone.
notes: Two narrations: the freed slave's account (the freed slave is unnamed) and the Sulaymaan bin Yasaar account (Sabeegh bin Isl of Banu Tameem). Sabeegh is not in the approved list and his sahabi status is not stated.

summary: Abu Uthmaan says Umar wrote ordering the Muslims not to associate with Sabeegh, and another narration says Sabeegh was despised by his people after once being their leader.
notes: Two reports: Abu Uthmaan's account of the boycott and an unattributed 'another narration'. The narrator is recorded as the approved 'abu-uthmaan' (unsure), which may not be the same person.

summary: Some men from Egypt, who had questioned Abdullaah bin Umar about difficult Qur'aanic matters, are examined by Umar on what they have memorised and practised, and Umar says he would have made an example of them if the people of Madinah had known.
notes: Narrator 'Hadhrat Hasan' has the same identity question as n02811. The men from Egypt are unnamed.

summary: Ubaadah bin Saamit says that a migrant he had taught the Qur'aan gave him a bow as a gift, and the Prophet called it a burning ember hung between his shoulders.
notes: The migrant is unnamed.

summary: Ubay bin Ka'b, having taught a Surah to a man who gave him a garment, is told by the Prophet that wearing it would be wearing a garment of fire.
notes: The man who gave the garment is unnamed.

summary: Another narration says that when Ubay bin Ka'b taught the Qur'aan to a man, he received a bow as a gift.
notes: Short variant report with no response from the Prophet.

summary: Tufayl bin Amr relates that Ubay bin Ka'b, who had been given a bow for teaching him the Qur'aan, wore it to the Prophet, who called it a spark from Jahannam; Ubay replied that they also eat their food, and the Prophet distinguished food prepared for others from food prepared specially for oneself.
notes: Unsure whose food Ubay means by 'their food' (the opening quotation mark is OCR-garbled).

summary: Awf bin Maalik reports that a man he had taught the Qur'aan gave him a bow, and the Prophet asked whether he wanted to meet Allaah carrying an ember of Jahannam on his back.
notes: Footnote debris (a citation to Ibn Jareer) in the middle is ignored. The man who gave the bow is unnamed.

summary: Muthanna bin Waa'il recounts Abdullaah bin Busr's report of a man who was given a bow for teaching a child the Qur'aan, and the Prophet told him to return it, asking whether he wanted a bow of fire around his neck.
notes: The man who gave the bow is unnamed. Muthanna is not on the approved list; the approved 'muthanna' is a different person.

summary: Umar objects when he hears that Sa'd plans to pay Qur'aan teachers an allowance, later tells a governor to give allowances by merit of family and companionship with the Prophet instead, and warns that those who take pay for teaching will see even adulterers enter Jannah before them.
notes: Several reports, plus the author's bracketed commentary at the end on whether teachers may take pay, which is not part of the narration. The Sa'd here is not identified (Sa'd bin Abi Waqqaas is possible but not stated), so the entry is a null name. The governor is unnamed.

summary: Ibn Abbaas warns Umar that the spread of the Qur'aan among the people will lead to disputes, and after Umar's anger he recites verses to explain his view, and Umar agrees that he is right.
notes: The Qur'aan verses are quoted by reference (Baqarah 204-207) and not reproduced in full.

summary: Abdullaah bin Ubayd bin Umayr relates that Ibn Abbaas warned Umar that the spread of the Qur'aan would cause disputes and then killing, and that Umar admitted he had understood the same but had been concealing it.
notes: The text ends mid-sentence ('concealing this from the'), so the narration is incomplete.

summary: Kinaanah Adawi relates that Umar asked his commanders for lists of the Huffaadh so he could send them out to teach, that Abu Moosa replied there were just over three hundred, and that Umar wrote to them on honouring and following the Qur'aan.
notes: Qais is the addressee of Umar's letter and is not matched to an approved entry. The text ends with OCR debris.

summary: Abu Kinaanah and Abul Aswad Daly each relate Abu Moosa's addresses to his Huffaadh and Qurraa, urging them to follow the Qur'aan and not let time harden their hearts, and reminding them they will be questioned about what they do.
notes: Two narrations: Abu Kinaanah's (follow the Qur'aan) and Abul Aswad Daly's (the Qurraa and the hardening of hearts, with two verses). 'close t. three hundred' is OCR for close to three hundred.

summary: Abdullaah bin Mas'ood tells the people of Kufa not to dispute about the Qur'aan, since it contains no contradictions, and recalls that the Prophet approved his recitation; other reports add his advice on the qualities of a man of the Qur'aan and on listening carefully.
notes: Three reports: the Kufa address, a student's report from Hamdaan (unnamed), and a closing 'another narration'.

summary: Abu Hurayrah relates that when a Bedouin asked the Prophet, in the middle of his narrating, when the Qiyaamah would come, the Prophet said it would come when trusts are misappropriated and authority is given to unworthy people.
notes: The Bedouin and the Sahabah who commented are unnamed.

summary: Waabisah recalls the Prophet's address on the Farewell Hajj, that the month, city, and the blood, wealth and honour of the Muslims are sacred until the Day they meet their Rabb, and that those present must convey it to those absent.
notes: Waabisah is not on the approved list.

summary: Makhool relates that Abu Umaamah told him and his companions that their sitting was a means for the Deen to reach them and that they must propagate it, and Saleem bin Aamir relates that Abu Ubaadah asked his listeners after each session to pass on what they had heard.
notes: Two reports: Makhool's (Abu Umaamah in Hims) and Saleem bin Aamir's (Abu Ubaadah). Several Abu Ubaydahs are approved, but the text does not say which Abu Ubaadah, so it is left as null.

summary: Abdullaah bin Abbaas relates the Prophet's du'aa for mercy on his successors, those who will narrate his Ahadeeth and teach them to the people.
Aasim bin Muhammad relates from his father that he saw Abu Hurayrah on a Jumu'ah standing at the pulpit narrating Ahadeeth until the Imaam emerged, and then sit down.
notes: Aasim's father, who is the direct witness, is unnamed. The Prophet is named only inside Abu Hurayrah's quoted opening words.

summary: Aslam relates that Umar refused to narrate Ahadeeth when asked for fear of adding or omitting a word, and Abdur Rahmaan bin Haatib says that Uthmaan narrated more thoroughly than any Sahabi but was very reluctant to do so.
notes: Two reports: Aslam's (about Umar) and Abdur Rahmaan bin Haatib's (about Uthmaan).

summary: Uthmaan explains that his reluctance to narrate Ahadeeth is not weak memory but fear of the Prophet's warning against those who attribute falsehoods to him, and another narration gives that warning in different words.
notes: The second sentence is a variant wording of the same warning ('Another narration quotes').

summary: Ali says that when narrating Ahadeeth he would rather fall from the sky than say what the Prophet did not say, but that in matters of war strategy such strictness need not apply.
notes: The jihaad theme is included for the war-strategy remark in the second half.

summary: Amr bin Maymoon and Masrooq each relate that Abdullaah bin Mas'ood sometimes went a whole year without narrating a Hadith, and that when he did he trembled and sweated, adding a qualification to what he attributed to the Prophet.
notes: Two reports: Amr bin Maymoon's and Masrooq's, which differ in detail.
